svg.font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Molt attribution version history
svg.desc: A timeline of one artifact's client attribution across validity time: a first version opened at ingest by workspace mapping, superseded by a second version detected by vector similarity with higher confidence, and finally closed by an erasure that records the removal as history rather than leaving a hole. Beside it are the constraints that keep the history honest and the as of query the certificate reads.
svg.text: Attribution as a version history
A mutable row answers what is true now. A version history also answers when the claim started, which is the question an auditor asks.
t0 first ingest
t1 evidence strengthens
t2 supersession
t3 erasure closes it
now
validity time, left to right
version 1 · method: workspace mapping
confidence 0.60. valid_from t0, valid_to t2, superseded_by version 2.
The claim itself was never edited. Only its end and its successor were written, each exactly once.
version 2 · method: vector similarity
confidence 0.93. valid_from t2, valid_to t3, superseded_by the closure the erasure wrote.
This is the version a sweep resolves against, so a superseded version can neither widen nor narrow the sweep.
closed by erasure
The binding removal is recorded as history rather than left as a hole, so the row still says
the client was once bound and says when that stopped being true.
The as of query
Given an artifact and a point in validity time, which client did
Molt hold it against, by what method, and with what confidence.
Served by a covering index over the artifact and the descending
validity bounds, so it is an index range with no row fetch.
What the certificate carries
The earliest validity start and the detection method for every
touched artifact, read before any disposition runs. That is the
field that answers how long the data was held, which a deletion
receipt on its own can never answer.
What holds the history honest
A partial unique index admits one
unsuperseded version per artifact and
client pair, so a history accumulates
while exactly one version stays current.
A total check pairs the validity end with
the superseding reference, so a closed
version cannot exist without naming its
successor, and an ordered interval check
refuses a version that ends before it
starts.
The writer's UPDATE privilege covers
those two columns and nothing else, so
the immutability of a stored claim is a
privilege fact.
Concurrency
Supersession is one atomic pair of
statements under serializable isolation:
close the current version, then insert
its successor. Two concurrent ingests
cannot both open a current version,
because the second commit aborts and
its retry finds the version it must
supersede.
